title: Additional Immersive Haptic Virtual Reality Training and Psychomotor Performance in Occlusal Rest Preparation: A Randomized Controlled Study in Preclinical Setting
content: Background/Objectives: Evidence on virtual reality haptic simulators (VRHS) in removable prosthodontics is scarce. This study evaluated whether additional haptic simulator training be-fore conventional phantom-head training improves occlusal rest preparation performance. Methods: Thirty fourth-year dental students were randomized to an Experimental Group (EG; simulator–phantom–simulator) or a Control Group (CG; phantom–simulator). Preparations were scored (0–5) by two calibrated evaluators assessing coded preparations, and execution time was recorded. The main transfer outcome was phantom-based performance; non-parametric tests were used. Student perceptions were collected with a six-item questionnaire. Results: Phan-tom-based scores did not differ significantly between groups (median 4.25 vs. 4.00; p = 0.053). In the final simulator assessment, the EG scored higher than the CG (median 3.00 vs. 2.00; p = 0.047; r = 0.37). Within the EG, simulator scores improved (median 2.00 vs. 3.00; p = 0.003) and execu-tion time decreased by 50.7% (p < 0.001). Twenty students (66.7%) completed the questionnaire; agreement was highest for ease of use and pre-use information (65% each) and lowest for the su-periority of simulated over phantom-based preparation (25%). Conclusions: Additional haptic simulator training did not significantly improve phantom-based performance. The advantages observed on the simulator may reflect greater practice time and interface familiarity. Studies with equivalent training exposure are needed in order to confirm these results.
